body.text: India’s next nutrition leap will require Anganwadis to move beyond delivering services and become platforms for behaviour change, community accountability, and child-centred care
Image Source: Getty Images

India’s nutrition story has entered a different phase. For decades, the central challenge was one of access: getting food, health services, growth monitoring and information to women and children at scale. POSHAN Abhiyaan represented an important shift in this journey. It brought political attention to nutrition, placed the first 1,000 days at the centre of the national agenda, invested in frontline capacity, introduced digital monitoring and sought to turn nutrition into a Jan Andolan.

There is evidence that this design has delivered. As per NFHS 6, long-term stunting has declined from 35.5 percent to 29.3 percent, and severe acute wasting has dropped notably from 7.7 percent to 5.2 percent. These are important gains. Yet, despite strong early breastfeeding practices, more than one-third of infants are not introduced to essential solid or semi-solid foods during critical growth periods. Overall nutrition indicators have improved, but 40.5 percent of children aged 6–8 months still miss the necessary transition to complementary foods alongside breastmilk.

The question for India’s nutrition system is no longer just whether services reach families, but whether they influence daily practices within those families. This is why the Rashtriya Poshan Maah theme, “Hamari Anganwadi, Hamari Jimmedari”, should be viewed as a call to rethink the Anganwadi model after fifty years of operation. India has built an extensive delivery network from Anganwadi workers and ASHAs to panchayats, schools and digital platforms, but the last‑mile model that shapes household decisions remains underdeveloped.

A child’s nutrition does not improve because data is entered on a dashboard; it improves when mothers take iron‑folic acid, when breastfeeding starts early, when complementary feeding begins on time, when diets diversify, when growth faltering is spotted quickly, and when someone trusted helps the family respond. This is where the Anganwadi becomes indispensable. One of the most important achievements of POSHAN Abhiyaan has been the expansion of the system’s ability to identify and reach beneficiaries. The Poshan Tracker, for example, has brought unprecedented digital visibility to service delivery. The World Bank describes it as a transformational shift from the earlier paper-based system, while the government now reports its use across the Anganwadi network. That said, an important distinction exists between tracking a beneficiary and understanding a beneficiary.

A child’s weight shows the outcome, not the reason behind it. The underlying issue could be limited dietary diversity, infrequent feeding, recurring illness, a mother’s lack of time, the cost of food, cultural norms, weak family support, poor sanitation, or simply the family’s difficulty in turning nutrition advice into an affordable, practical meal.
The role of technology should therefore be to free frontline workers to do more of what technology cannot do: listen, counsel, demonstrate, follow up and build trust.

The next generation of India’s nutrition system needs to answer these questions. Otherwise, there exists a risk that the digital transformation of nutrition becomes primarily a transformation of reporting, rather than outcomes. The role of technology should therefore be to free frontline workers to do more of what technology cannot do: listen, counsel, demonstrate, follow up and build trust.

India has made substantial progress in breastfeeding, but studies show complementary feeding remains a major weak link. This gap becomes especially critical once a child crosses six months. Families don’t need another broad reminder to “give nutritious food.” They need practical guidance: which foods to offer, in what quantity, how often, whether it fits their budget, how to prepare it with local ingredients, whether the child will accept it, and what alternatives to use when something isn’t available. A demonstration of how to make a protein-rich meal from locally available ingredients can sometimes be more powerful than a poster listing ten nutrition messages. A mother cooking with an Anganwadi worker can be more consequential than a counselling session consisting of instructions. A father’s participation in that conversation can be more impactful than another leaflet.

There is another implication of the 2026 theme that deserves greater attention. “Hamari Anganwadi, Hamari Jimmedari” should not become a new way of placing more responsibility on an already stretched frontline worker. It should mean precisely the opposite: responsibility moves from the individual worker to the community.

The government is already signalling this direction through the proposed operationalisation of Anganwadi Management Committees and greater involvement of parents, panchayats, Self-Help Groups (SHGs), and mothers’ groups. The revised supplementary nutrition guidelines also emphasise transparency around menus and the quality of hot cooked meals.

The opportunity now is to make these mechanisms functional rather than merely institutional. An effective system must be able to assess whether children are receiving the intended food, ensure that menus are locally acceptable, confirm that pregnant and lactating women are adequately supported, track follow-up for children who are not growing well, evaluate whether the centre is accessible and welcoming, determine the extent of mothers’ participation, identify the barriers families report, and clarify what issues the panchayat or community can address. This would transform accountability from reporting upwards to problem-solving locally.

India’s nutrition monitoring and surveillance systems have become more sophisticated, but the metrics we choose still shape system behaviour. When we track only how many children are weighed, the system prioritises weighing. When we count counselling sessions, it produces more sessions. But when we measure whether vulnerable children get the care they need, the system must ask a different question: what does each child need to truly get better?

The next generation of nutrition indicators must increasingly capture continuity of care and the system’s response. They should track whether mothers were counselled after growth faltering was detected, whether follow‑up visits occurred, whether households adopted recommended practices, whether dietary diversity improved, whether referrals were made when necessary, and whether the child ultimately recovered.

Therefore, the next generation of nutrition indicators must increasingly capture continuity of care and the system’s response. They should track whether mothers were counselled after growth faltering was detected, whether follow‑up visits occurred, whether households adopted recommended practices, whether dietary diversity improved, whether referrals were made when necessary, and whether the child ultimately recovered. This does not imply abandoning coverage indicators; rather, it requires shifting from a transactional measurement system to one that is genuinely outcome‑oriented.

The strongest nutrition efforts succeed because beneficiaries are not treated as passive recipients. Mothers participate, frontline workers demonstrate, children engage, families ask questions, and communities adapt messages to local realities. Local foods become part of the solution, and the Anganwadi becomes a place people want to visit. This reflects Jan Andolan at the last mile and underscores why nutrition and early childhood development must go hand in hand. With initiatives like Poshan Bhi Padhai Bhi, India is moving toward an integrated Anganwadi model centred on the child.
If the Anganwadi is to become a genuine development platform, five shifts are needed.
• First, from beneficiary coverage to child trajectories.
• Second, from nutrition messaging to nutrition practice
• Third, from frontline-worker accountability to frontline-worker enablement.
• Fourth, from community participation to community accountability.
• Fifth, from schemes to a child-centred continuum.
India has proven it can build nutrition systems at scale, but the next step is making national programmes responsive to local realities.
